quote: the schema, the queries, and the storage layout were entangled
problem: The reader has never met 'schema' (it appears nowhere in Parts I to III and is not explained here), so they cannot name the first of the three tangled things, and Codd's whole complaint of brittleness rests on how those three depend on each other.
fix: a plain gloss such as 'the declared shape of the records: which kinds exist and which fields each has'
reason: 'Schema' appears nowhere in Parts I to III and its first use (ch13-codd-p2) is the load-bearing word of Codd's complaint; ch13-sql-p2 then uses it again as the thing DDL changes, still unglossed. A real gap for the baseline reader.
judge_fix: ch13-codd-p2: 'the schema (which kinds of records exist and which fields each has), the queries, and the storage layout were entangled, and changing any one broke the others.' That one gloss also covers ch13-sql-p2.

quote: the same rows with far fewer of them to join (Fig 13.3 shows it)
problem: Fig 13.3 is not in this section. It is in Section 03 (ch13-sql) and the text is not a link, so the reader stops to hunt for a figure they have not reached yet. The prose already carries the rule without it (the figure comes later, at fig-13-3 in ch13-sql).
fix: '(Fig 13.3, in Section 03, shows it)' or make it a link
reason: Verified: Fig 13.3 sits in ch13-sql (Section 03), not in Section 02, and the reference is plain text. Section cross-references of the form 'Section 03' are already the book's convention (ch13-algebra-p4), so the fix is free and consistent.
judge_fix: ch13-algebra-p6: '(Fig 13.3, in Section 03, shows it)'.

quote: an index on age only if few rows pass
problem: The reader has not been told what a database index is, so cannot see why it is only worth using when few rows pass and why a full scan wins otherwise. (Indexes are not explained anywhere in this section; 'CREATE INDEX' in p2 is only a name.)
fix: one plain clause: an index jumps straight to the matching rows, but each jump is a separate read, so when most rows match, one straight pass is cheaper
reason: 'Index' is first explained in Section 05 (ch13-indexes-p1), two sections after Fig 13.3's strip and ch13-sql-p2's CREATE INDEX. The strip's 'only if few rows pass' cannot be followed without knowing what an index does. Best repair is a short gloss plus forward pointer at the strip, not a long explanation.
judge_fix: Fig 13.3 strip, 'The choices': 'an index on age (a lookup shortcut, Section 05) pays only if few rows pass, because each match costs a separate jump (here nearly everyone is an adult, so scanning wins), a hash join when both inputs are large (Fig 13.4).'

id: fig-13-4 (How it works, 'Nested loop' and 'Merge join')
quote: the inner side has an index on the join key
problem: Indexes are still unexplained, so the reader cannot see why one 'index lookup' replaces a scan of the whole inner table, or why an index hands the merge join its rows already sorted.
fix: the same short gloss of an index (a sorted lookup structure that finds a key without scanning), given once at its first use
reason: Same root gap as finding 6: the Fig 13.4 strip uses 'index on the join key' and 'from an index' before Section 05. It needs only the pointer once finding 6's gloss exists; no separate long explanation.
judge_fix: Fig 13.4 strip: 'the inner side has an index on the join key (Section 05)' and 'for example from an index (Section 05)'. The gloss from finding 6 serves as the single definition.

quote: snapshot isolation still allows write skew, which only serializable prevents.
problem: This is in Fig 13.7's How it works strip. It says PostgreSQL's repeatable read already blocks all three anomalies in the table, so the only thing left for serializable is 'write skew', which the book never explains. 'Snapshot isolation' only becomes readable at p8. The reader can no longer say what serializable adds, and p8's Serializable abort rule then has no example of the overlap it catches.
fix: drop the write-skew clause, or give one plain two-transaction example at p8
reason: Fig 13.7's strip leaves the reader with 'only serializable prevents write skew' and the term appears nowhere else in the book, so what serializable adds over PostgreSQL's repeatable read is unexplained. Facts are right (PostgreSQL RR is snapshot isolation, blocks phantoms, still allows write skew; SSI prevents it). Fix by one concrete example, not by cutting.
judge_fix: Fig 13.7 strip, 'The table is a minimum': 'PostgreSQL's repeatable read is snapshot isolation and blocks phantoms too; it still lets two overlapping transactions each check a rule against the same snapshot and both break it (two doctors each go off call, each seeing the other still on duty), and only serializable prevents that.'

quote: A lookup descends from the root, one page per level, to the leaf
problem: The reader cannot say how a lookup picks which child to read at each level, or why 15, 30 and 45 appear both in an upper node and again in a leaf. The old caption carried this step (internal nodes route lookups by comparing the sought key against theirs; the leaves hold the real key and row-pointer pairs), and now only the numbers in the drawing do, so a newcomer has to work it out from the picture (20 < 30 goes left, 20 ≥ 15 goes right).
fix: one clause: an upper node's keys are signposts (smaller goes left, equal or larger right), copies of keys whose rows sit in the leaves, which is also why hundreds of keys mean hundreds of children
reason: The B-tree prose says only 'one page per level from root to leaf'. How a page's keys pick the child, and why 15, 30, 45 recur in the leaves, is carried only by the numbers in the drawing (I checked the t8 frame: nothing labels the routing). That is the mechanism, so law 4 'never too shallow' applies. The caption is already at its sentence limit, so the clause goes in p2.
judge_fix: ch13-indexes-p2, after 'reads one page per level from root to leaf': ', the keys in each upper page acting as signposts (below this key go left, at or above it go right) with the real keys and their rows in the leaves'.

quote: range queries (`WHERE id BETWEEN 100 AND 200`) cannot use the index
problem: The reader has just learned that one key is found by hashing it, so they cannot see why a range of whole numbers (100 to 200 here, 40 to 45 in Fig 13.9) is not found by hashing each value in turn. 'Cannot use the index' and the caption's 'the only way to find them is to look in every one' therefore do not follow from what was said.
fix: a clause: most ranges hold values that cannot be listed one by one (any name from Al to Am, any price from 10 to 20), so only an ordered index can walk them
reason: A reader who just learned 'hash the key, go to the slot' can fairly ask why 100..200 is not simply 101 lookups; for whole numbers it could be. 'No way to walk neighbours' and the caption's 'the only way is to look in every one' do not by themselves rule that out. The general reason (ranges over values nobody can list) is the true one.
judge_fix: ch13-indexes-p4: '...cannot use the index: the hashed positions are scattered across the array, with no way to walk neighbours (and a range can hold values nobody could look up one by one, such as every name from Al to Am).'

quote: an apostrophe in the input terminates the developer's quoted string
problem: The book never says that SQL puts a text value between apostrophes and ends it at the next apostrophe. It showed status='paid' and LIKE 'Al%' without stating that rule. Fig 13.10's code also mixes the program's double quotes with SQL's single quotes. So this reader cannot explain why an apostrophe the user types ends a string the developer wrote, and may take 'the developer's quoted string' to mean the double-quoted pieces.
fix: one sentence in p2, since the figure is kept original: SQL writes a text value between apostrophes (name='alice') and reads it up to the next apostrophe. Once the pieces are glued together, the database gets one line and cannot tell which apostrophes the user typed
reason: The book never states that SQL puts text between apostrophes and reads it up to the next one, and Fig 13.10 mixes program double quotes with SQL single quotes. A non-programmer cannot tell which 'quoted string' the caption means. Fig 13.10 is kept-original, so the repair goes in the lead-in p2, not the figure.
judge_fix: ch13-injection-p2: 'Suppose a login form takes a username and password and builds the query by string concatenation. SQL writes a text value between apostrophes (name='alice') and reads it up to the next apostrophe; once the pieces are glued together, the database receives one line and cannot tell which apostrophes the user typed:'

quote: Parameterised queries close the primary vulnerability, but a serious application stacks more layers
problem: p4 called this defence 'clean and absolute', so this reader cannot see why more layers are needed or how that layer could 'fail' (the strip's last line says 'even when one layer fails'). The missing step: the fix only protects the queries written with it, and one query built by hand anywhere in the code reopens the hole.
fix: half a sentence: because one query still built by hand anywhere in the program reopens the hole
reason: p4 calls the defence 'clean and absolute', the strip says it needs more layers and that a layer may 'fail', with no stated reason. The missing step is that the fix protects only queries written with it. Half a sentence removes the apparent contradiction.
judge_fix: ch13-injection-p6: 'Parameterised queries close the primary vulnerability, but a serious application stacks more layers, because one query still built by hand anywhere in the program reopens the hole.'

quote: a driver that only emulates this must escape every value correctly instead
problem: This reader knows 'driver' only as the kernel code that runs a piece of hardware (ch4-anatomy), and 'escape' was never explained in plain words (it appears only as 'HTML-escape' in the kept-original Fig 12.9). So this caveat to an 'absolute' defence cannot be followed: some libraries only pretend to send values separately and fall back on marking apostrophes in the text.
fix: gloss driver as 'the library a program uses to talk to the database' and escape as 'mark each apostrophe so the parser reads it as a letter'
reason: In the Fig 13.11 strip 'driver' (a kernel/hardware word in Part II) and 'escape' (never explained in plain words) carry the only caveat to an 'absolute' defence. Plain-language swap keeps the strip short.
judge_fix: Fig 13.11 strip, 'On the wire': '...send the statement and its parameters as separate messages; a database library that only emulates this has to escape every value itself (mark each apostrophe so the parser reads it as a letter).'

quote: the SQL text, a placeholder where each value goes, is parsed once
problem: Read as written, the phrase in commas says the SQL text is a placeholder. The reader has to re-read and check the picture to see that the text contains a placeholder for each value.
fix: 'the SQL text, with a placeholder where each value goes,'
reason: Genuine apposition ambiguity in the Fig 13.11 caption: 'the SQL text, a placeholder where each value goes,' reads as 'the SQL text is a placeholder'. The caption is not owner text. One-word repair.
judge_fix: ch13-injection-p5: 'With a parameterised query the SQL text, with a placeholder where each value goes, is parsed once into a plan, and the values travel separately and are bound into it afterwards.'

quote: which on two million-row tables is a trillion of them, minutes of work.
problem: A trillion row comparisons takes hours in a real database engine, not minutes. I timed a SQLite nested-loop join (10,000 x 10,000 rows, in memory, automatic index off) at about 20 ns per comparison, which extrapolates to about 5.7 hours for 10^12. Even a bare C loop at 1 ns per comparison needs about 17 minutes. The chapter's own rate also disagrees: ch13-indexes-p1 says a 10-million-row scan takes 'seconds', which puts 10^12 row visits at roughly a day.
fix: "which on two million-row tables is a trillion of them, hours of work."
reason: A nested-loop join over 10^12 pairs costs hours in a real engine (about 20 ns per comparison gives roughly 5 to 6 hours; even a bare 1 ns loop is about 17 minutes). 'Minutes' is wrong for a database, and the chapter's own 'seconds' per 10-million-row scan implies longer still. The caption and figure make no time claim, so only p4 needs the change.
judge_fix: ch13-sql-p4: "...which on two million-row tables is a trillion of them, hours of work."

quote: He spent his last decade increasingly frustrated that commercial databases, IBM's included, implemented incomplete versions of his model
problem: This puts the frustration in the wrong period. Codd died in April 2003, and during the 1990s his health declined and he stopped working (Wikipedia, Edgar F. Codd). His fight over the word 'relational' was in the 1980s: the 1985 Computerworld rules named in the next sentence and RM/V2 in 1990. Read together, the two sentences place 1985 inside his 'last decade'.
fix: "From the 1980s on he grew increasingly frustrated that commercial databases, IBM's included, implemented incomplete versions of his model ..."
reason: Codd's fight over the word 'relational' was in the 1980s (the 1985 Computerworld rules, RM/V2 in 1990). He died in 2003, so 'last decade' places the 1985 rules outside it. The paragraph is an insight strip, not owner text.
judge_fix: ch13-codd-p8: "In the years that followed he grew increasingly frustrated that commercial databases, IBM's included, implemented incomplete versions of his model and used \"relational\" as a marketing term for systems that were not quite."

quote: Serializable also tracks which transactions read data that others wrote
problem: This names the wrong conflict. PostgreSQL's Serializable Snapshot Isolation watches for read-write antidependencies: a transaction reads a row version that a concurrent transaction is overwriting, so the reader never sees that write. Reading data that another transaction wrote and committed is normal and harmless. As worded, the sentence suggests the opposite case is the one being tracked.
fix: "Serializable also tracks which transactions read data that a concurrent transaction was changing, and aborts ..."
reason: Serializable Snapshot Isolation tracks read-write dependencies, where a reader reads a version that a concurrent transaction is overwriting. 'Read data that others wrote' describes ordinary committed reads, so it names the wrong direction. This is low severity but the repair is a few words.
judge_fix: ch13-acid-p8: "...and Serializable also tracks which concurrent transactions read data that another was changing, and aborts (cancels and rolls back) one of them whenever their overlap could produce a result..." (rest unchanged)

quote: Called Ingres, it became the basis for the open-source Postgres (1986)
problem: 'Basis' implies Postgres was built from Ingres's code. It was not. Postgres was Stonebraker's new 'post-Ingres' project, begun after he returned to Berkeley in 1985, with implementation starting in 1986. It was a fresh code base that took ideas, not code, from Ingres, and its query language was PostQUEL until Postgres95 (PostgreSQL docs, 'A Brief History of PostgreSQL'; Wikipedia, PostgreSQL). Fig 13.1's 'Ingres led to Postgres' is accurate; the prose goes further than the figure.
fix: "Called Ingres, it led to Stonebraker's successor project, Postgres (1986), which became PostgreSQL (1996), and indirectly to Sybase ..."
reason: Postgres (1986) was Stonebraker's new post-Ingres project, a fresh code base that reused ideas and not code, so 'became the basis for' overstates. Fig 13.1 already says 'led to'. 'Open-source' for 1986 is also anachronistic; it fits PostgreSQL (1996). Findings 4 and 9 are the same defect and take one fix.
judge_fix: ch13-codd-p6: "Called *Ingres*, it led to Stonebraker's successor project, _Postgres_ (1986), which became the open-source _PostgreSQL_ (1996), and, through its alumni, to _Sybase_, which Microsoft licensed and turned into _SQL Server_." Source: PostgreSQL docs, 'A Brief History of PostgreSQL'.

quote: DML (Data Manipulation Language) changes the data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
problem: SELECT reads data and changes nothing, so it cannot be an example of a statement that 'changes the data'. The DDL half of the sentence is right ('changes the schema').
fix: "DML (Data Manipulation Language) reads and changes the data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE."
reason: SELECT reads and does not change data, so it cannot be an example under 'changes the data'. The DDL half of the sentence is right. Same defect as finding 15.
judge_fix: ch13-sql-p2: "*DML* (Data Manipulation Language) reads and changes the _data_: `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`."

quote: the 2011 Sony PlayStation Network breach (77 million)
problem: The 77 million were PlayStation Network accounts, not payment cards. Placed straight after 'Heartland breach (130 million payment cards)', the bare number reads as 77 million cards. Sony said card data was on file for far fewer accounts. This is only about the unit. The owner's ruling to keep PSN in the SQL injection list is not touched.
fix: "the 2011 Sony PlayStation Network breach (77 million accounts)"
reason: The point is right: 77 million were PSN accounts, and the bare number after 'Heartland (130 million payment cards)' reads as cards. But the sentence sits in the caption of fig-13-10, a kept-original figure whose Sony claim is already an owner call (docs/pass-30-figures.md, UNDER.md §4g). Only the owner can change it.
judge_fix: If the owner agrees: "the 2011 Sony PlayStation Network breach (77 million accounts)".

problem: ch13-codd-p6: Postgres (1986) was a new system Stonebraker started as the successor to Ingres. It was not built on Ingres's code, so 'became the basis for' overstates; the figure's 'led to' is accurate. Calling it 'open-source' in 1986 is also anachronistic: the code was released under a BSD-style licence from 1989.
reason: Same defect as finding 4: 'became the basis for' overstates Postgres's relation to Ingres, and 'open-source' is anachronistic for 1986. One fix covers both.
judge_fix: See finding 4 (ch13-codd-p6 replacement sentence).

problem: ch13-codd-p8: 'He spent his last decade increasingly frustrated': Codd died in 2003, but the evidence given (the 1985 rules) and his RM/V2 book (1990) both come well before his last decade (1993 to 2003). 'His later years' would fit the evidence.
reason: Same defect as finding 2. Codd's last decade was 1993 to 2003, and the evidence the paragraph gives dates from 1985 and 1990.
judge_fix: See finding 2 (ch13-codd-p8: "In the years that followed he grew increasingly frustrated...").

problem: ch13-algebra-p3: 'queries that follow a chain of any length, a manager's manager's manager ... sit outside it'. A chain of fixed length three can be written with two self-joins, which is exactly what the rename sentence just before shows. What falls outside the algebra is a chain of unknown length (every manager up to the top, however many levels). The example as written reads as if three levels were already impossible. Suggest 'every manager above someone, however many levels up'.
reason: A chain of fixed length three is just two self-joins, which the rename sentence in the same paragraph has just shown. What lies outside the algebra is a chain of unknown length, which SQL later added through recursion. As written, 'a manager's manager's manager' reads as if three levels were already impossible, which a careful reader would catch.
judge_fix: ch13-algebra-p3, the parenthesis: "(counting, totals and queries that follow a chain of unknown length, such as every manager above someone however many levels up, which SQL later adds, sit outside it)"

problem: ch13-sql-p2: 'DML changes the data' lists SELECT, but SELECT only reads. Some texts file it separately as DQL. The sentence is wrong as written for one of its four examples.
reason: Duplicate of finding 5: SELECT is listed under a sentence saying DML 'changes the data'.
judge_fix: See finding 5 ("...reads and changes the _data_...").

problem: fig-13-10 caption (kept original): Sony never confirmed that its 2011 PlayStation Network breach (77 million) was SQL injection. The LulzSec breach of Sony Pictures the same year was. Already logged as an owner call in docs/pass-30-figures.md and UNDER.md §4g, so it is noted here only so the list is complete.
reason: fig-13-10 is a kept-original figure. The Sony PSN SQL-injection claim is already logged as an owner call in docs/pass-30-figures.md line 96 and UNDER.md §4g, and the owner decided to leave it in place. Nothing new for the owner to decide.
judge_fix: No change unless the owner reverses the earlier call.

problem: fig-13-10 (kept original): the vulnerable login query compares pw directly with the typed password, which means passwords are stored as plain text. Yet the UNION payload line says it 'exfiltrates every password hash'. If pw held hashes, the query as drawn would never match a real login. The figure contradicts itself here. Minor.
reason: Real but minor inconsistency in a kept-original figure: the vulnerable code compares pw to the typed password (plain text), while the UNION payload line says it exfiltrates 'every password hash'. Only the owner can touch it. The inconsistency would not block a reader.
judge_fix: If the owner wants it fixed: change the payload note to "exfiltrates every stored password".

quote: consistent: T42 kept, T43 gone
problem: Fig 13.6 uses Fig 13.5's people and amounts but splits the transfer into two transactions: T42 debits Alice 100, T43 pays Bob 100. Its end state, Alice €100 and Bob €50 (total €150), is exactly the state Fig 13.5, two figures earlier, marks in red as '€100 has vanished'. Here that state is labelled 'consistent'. A reader who has just learned that a transfer is one atomic transaction sees money vanish and be called correct.
fix: Redraw T43 on a third account so neither transaction is half of the Alice-to-Bob transfer. For example: 'T43 Cara 80 → 30', Cara's page written early and undone back to €80. Alternatively, let T42 carry both halves of the transfer (Alice 200 → 100, Bob 50 → 150, commit) and make T43 an uncommitted second transfer. Update the <desc> and the caption to match.
reason: Verified in the SVG text: T42 Alice 200 to 100 committed, T43 Bob 50 to 150 uncommitted, end state Alice 100 and Bob 50, labelled 'consistent'. That is the half-transfer state Fig 13.5 marks 'a hundred euros vanished'. The finding's first fix (T43 on a third account) still leaves T42 as a committed lone debit of Alice with Bob unpaid, so it does not remove the contradiction.
judge_fix: Text-only edit: make both transactions unrelated single-row ones on fresh accounts. Labels: 'T42  Cara 80 → 130', 'T42  commit', 'T43  Dan 20 → 70'; pages 'Cara' €80 (stale) → €130 (redo), 'Dan' €70 (dirty) → €20 (undo); status line "Cara's page stale, Dan's dirty"; keep 'recovery: redo T42, undo T43' and 'consistent: T42 kept, T43 gone'. Update the <desc> to 'Transaction 42 raises Cara from 80 to 130 and commits ... Transaction 43 raises Dan from 20 to 70 without committing, and Dan's page is written early ... redoes 42 so Cara's page says 130, undoes 43 so Dan's says 20 again.' The caption (ch13-acid-p5) names nobody, so it stays.

quote: O(|R| × |S|), yet the right choice when one side is tiny
problem: The strip writes all three costs in Big-O with |R| and |S| bars: O(|R| × |S|), O(|R| + |S|), O(|R| + |S|). Big-O is first explained two sections later, in ch13-indexes-p1, and the bar notation is never explained. Pass 30's handover listed this (docs/pass-30-figures.md) and it is still open.
fix: Nested loop: "Work grows with the product of the two table sizes, yet the right choice when one side is tiny or …". Hash join: "Work grows with the sum of the two sizes, for equality joins, if …". Merge join: "Also the sum, after sorting, so it wins when …".
reason: Big-O is first explained in ch13-indexes-p1 (Section 05); the Fig 13.4 strip in Section 03 uses O(|R| × |S|) with bar notation nowhere explained. Part II uses O(log N) only in passing, without a gloss. Already listed as open in docs/pass-30-figures.md.
judge_fix: Nested loop: "Work grows with the product of the two table sizes, yet it is the right choice when one side is tiny or the inner side has an index on the join key, so each outer row costs one index lookup." Hash join: "Work grows with the sum of the two sizes, for equality joins, if the smaller side's hash table fits in memory; otherwise it is split into partitions on disk." Merge join: "Also the sum, after sorting, so it wins when the inputs already arrive sorted, for example from an index. The optimiser picks among the three from table sizes, indexes and the join condition."

quote: a result that running them one after the other, in any order, could not
problem: The sentence on Serializable stacks two parentheticals and ends on an elliptical 'could not' (could not produce). It has to be read twice for its syntax, in a paragraph the owner-read map sends him to (ch13-acid-p8).
fix: "…Repeatable Read one per transaction. Serializable also watches which transactions read data that others wrote: when two overlap in a way no one-after-the-other order could reproduce, it aborts (cancels and rolls back) one of them, sometimes more often than strictly needed."
reason: The Serializable sentence in ch13-acid-p8 stacks two parentheticals and ends on an elliptical 'could not'. It does need two reads. Note the original says 'could produce' (the engine aborts on a possible anomaly), so the fix must keep that sense. The same rewrite lowercases the level names (see 37).
judge_fix: Replace from 'PostgreSQL uses MVCC throughout' to the end of that sentence with: "PostgreSQL uses MVCC throughout: read committed takes a fresh snapshot per statement, repeatable read one per transaction, and serializable also tracks which transactions read data that others wrote. When two of them overlap in a way that might give a result no one-after-the-other order could, it aborts (cancels and rolls back) one, even though the overlap was sometimes harmless."

quote: a manager's manager's manager, which SQL later adds, sit outside it
problem: In 'That is what relationally complete means (counting, totals and queries that follow a chain of any length, a manager's manager's manager, which SQL later adds, sit outside it)', the parenthetical has its own subject, an appositive and a relative clause, all set off by commas. The reader cannot find the verb on the first pass.
fix: "That is what relationally complete means. Counting, totals and chains of any length (a manager's manager's manager) sit outside it; SQL added them later." Then end the paragraph there (see the next finding).
reason: The parenthetical in ch13-algebra-p3 carries its own subject, an appositive and a relative clause, and the verb 'sit' arrives last. Reads badly on first pass. Together with 5, the paragraph should end here.
judge_fix: "That is what relationally complete means. Counting, totals and chains of any length (a manager's manager's manager) sit outside it; SQL added them later." End the paragraph there.

quote: the join (⨝) is shorthand for a cross product followed by a selection.
problem: 'Join = product + selection' is said four times in one section: p1 ('the last of them derived from the others'), the Fig 13.2 strip ('a join is a product followed by a selection'), p3 itself ('bolt a selection onto it and you have rebuilt the join from parts') and again at the end of p3. The strip also calls it 'Cartesian product' where p3 says 'cross product'.
fix: Cut p3's closing clause '; the join (⨝) is shorthand for a cross product followed by a selection'. Cut the Fig 13.2 strip bullet 'The rest of the algebra': p3 names all six operators and rebuilds the join.
reason: p3 says the product-plus-selection join twice in one paragraph ('rebuilt the join from parts' and the closing '; the join is shorthand for a cross product followed by a selection'), and the Fig 13.2 strip bullet says it a third time, one paragraph above. The count of four is slightly inflated (p1 only says the join is derived), but the closing clause is a pure repeat and the strip bullet just lists what p3 names. The strip also says 'Cartesian product' where p3 says 'cross product'.
judge_fix: Cut p3's closing clause (already gone with the fix to 4). Cut the Fig 13.2 strip bullet 'The rest of the algebra'. Keep 'In SQL.' and 'Sets and bags' decisions as in 19.

quote: Filtering first gives the same answer with fewer rows to join: σ(R ⨝ S) = σ(R) ⨝ S
problem: Selection pushdown is explained twice, in two sections. ch13-algebra-p6 states the rule with the same formula and points to Fig 13.3. Here the caption ('moves the age filter below the join, so only adults are joined') and this strip bullet repeat it.
fix: Cut the 'The rewrite' bullet. The caption and ch13-algebra-p6 already carry the rule.
reason: The Fig 13.3 strip bullet 'The rewrite' repeats the formula σ(R ⨝ S) = σ(R) ⨝ S and its condition nearly verbatim from ch13-algebra-p6 (which also points to Fig 13.3), and the caption already says it in words beside the drawing.
judge_fix: Cut the 'The rewrite' bullet. Keep 'The choices' and 'Seeing it'.

quote: the major relational databases still running descend from one or the other
problem: The lineage is said three times: ch13-codd-p6 ('the major databases in production in 2026 either descend from one of two 1970s prototypes…'), this caption, and the strip ('MySQL and SQLite were written fresh, but speak the same SQL'). The brief says the prose keeps the explanation and the caption names the picture.
fix: Caption: "Two family trees from one paper, System R at IBM and Ingres at Berkeley; the dashed lines mark Oracle borrowing IBM's published SQL and Ingres alumni founding Sybase." Cut the strip's last sentence ('MySQL and SQLite were written fresh, but speak the same SQL').
reason: Only half holds. The strip's last sentence 'MySQL and SQLite were written fresh, but speak the same SQL' repeats ch13-codd-p6 and is not drawn in the picture. The caption, however, names exactly what the tree draws (the solid and dashed lines), so rewriting it is taste.
judge_fix: Cut only the last sentence of the 'Berkeley's side' strip bullet. Leave the caption unchanged.

quote: Since a value never reaches the parser, nothing in it can change what the query does
problem: The caption repeats ch13-injection-p4 ('Whatever the attacker sends as a value … stays data and is never parsed as code'). p4 itself then restates the point a second time, 'The predicate is always exactly what the developer wrote.', using 'predicate', a word this chapter's prose never explains.
fix: Cut p4's last sentence. Caption: "The SQL text, with a slot for the value, is parsed once into a plan; O'Brien, then Smith, is bound into the slot without passing the parser, its apostrophe only a letter."
reason: Only the p4 half holds. p4's last sentence 'The predicate is always exactly what the developer wrote' restates the sentence before it and uses 'predicate', which the chapter prose never defines (Fig 13.10, a kept original, uses it in its drawing). The caption's 'an apostrophe is only a letter' names the picture and should stay.
judge_fix: Cut p4's last sentence. Leave the Fig 13.11 caption unchanged.

quote: None of these alone is sufficient; together they make SQL injection rare even when one layer fails.
problem: The heading says 'The fix · parameterised queries · and only that' and p4 calls the defence 'clean and absolute'. This closing line then says 'none of these alone is sufficient', which a reader can take to include parameterised queries. 'Rare even when one layer fails' is also muddled: the extra layers limit the damage, they do not make injection rarer.

reason: The section heading says 'parameterised queries · and only that' and p4 says 'clean and absolute'; the closing line 'None of these alone is sufficient; together they make SQL injection rare even when one layer fails' can be read to include parameterised queries, and 'rare' is imprecise (least privilege limits damage, it does not make injection rarer).

quote: each permitting more anomalies in exchange for more concurrency

quote: was invented for IBM's System R by Patricia Selinger and described in a 1979 paper at SIGMOD
problem: A 33-word relative clause separates the subject ('The optimiser-as-component') from its verb. 'that is among the most cited' then attaches to 'conference' rather than 'paper'. The next sentence restates the first ('choose the plan by its estimated cost, using statistics about the data'). The owner-read map sends him here.

It estimates each plan's cost from statistics about the tables and finds the cheapest join order by working out the best way to join each small group of tables, then building up. Her 1979 paper at SIGMOD, the main database research conference ("Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System"), is among the most cited on query optimisation. Every cost-based optimiser since (…) builds on that idea."
reason: One sentence of about 80 words separates 'The optimiser-as-component' from 'was invented', and 'that is among the most cited' attaches to the conference. The next sentence restates the first. judge_fix: "Patricia Selinger and her colleagues at IBM designed the cost-based optimiser for System R. It estimates each plan's cost from statistics about the tables, and finds the cheapest join order by working out the best way to join each small group of tables first and building up from there. Their 1979 paper at SIGMOD, the main database research conference (_\"Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System\"_), is among the most cited on query optimisation, and every cost-based optimiser since (Oracle's, PostgreSQL's, SQL Server's, the cloud warehouses') builds on it. Forty-seven years on, in 2026, the paper is still required reading in graduate database courses for the same reason Codd's is: both were definitive on first publication."
